units.t: Hands-On Life Skills. Episode one.
In this episode: DIY basics: your toolkit and first fixes, Six knots worth knowing, Mending clothes: buttons, seams and holes and Cleaning smarter: the science of stains.
Part one. DIY basics: your toolkit and first fixes.
Hanging a mirror, patching a hole and fixing a sticking door are well within reach.
Knowing which jobs to leave to a licensed tradie is just as important.
Build a starter toolkit.
You do not need a shed full of gear to look after a home.
A good starter kit fits in one toolbox.
Include a claw hammer, screwdrivers with both flat and Phillips heads, a tape measure, a spirit level, a utility knife with spare blades, pliers and an adjustable spanner.
A cordless drill driver is the single most useful power tool, since it both drills holes and drives screws.
Add a stud finder, a pencil, sandpaper, a putty knife and a selection of screws and wall plugs.
Safety gear belongs in the kit too: safety glasses, gloves and a dust mask.
Buy decent quality basics rather than a giant bargain set of flimsy tools, and keep everything together so you are not hunting for the hammer every time.
Know your limits.
Most DIY injuries come from ordinary moments: a slip on a ladder, a chip of masonry in the eye.
Wear safety glasses whenever you drill, hammer or cut, and keep three points of contact on ladders.
Remove the battery before changing bits or blades.
In homes built or renovated before 2004, some materials may contain asbestos, including some wall and ceiling sheeting, eaves and vinyl floor tiles.
You cannot identify it by looking, so do not drill, cut or sand anything you suspect, and get it tested.
In every state and territory, electrical wiring work, including replacing a power point, must be done by a licensed electrician.
Gas fitting needs a licensed gasfitter, and most plumbing needs a licensed plumber.
Unlicensed work can be dangerous, illegal and may affect your insurance.
Drilling into walls.
Most Australian homes have plasterboard walls fixed to timber or steel studs, commonly spaced about 450 or 600 millimetres apart.
Pipes and electrical cables also run inside.
Cables often travel straight up or down from power points and switches, so avoid drilling directly above or below them.
A stud finder with cable detection helps, but it is not foolproof, so drill carefully and stop if you hit something unexpected.
For heavy items such as shelves, mirrors and wall mounted televisions, screw into the studs where possible.
Where there is no stud, use plasterboard anchors rated for the weight, as an ordinary screw will simply pull out.
Brick and concrete walls need a masonry drill bit and wall plugs.
Patching holes, fixing doors.
For small holes and dents in plasterboard, press ready mixed filler into the hole with a putty knife and scrape it level.
Many fillers shrink as they dry, so a second thin coat may be needed.
Once dry, sand gently, wipe off the dust and paint to match.
Holes bigger than a coin need a self adhesive mesh patch first.
Renters should check their lease before making holes.
A squealing door usually needs lubricant on the hinge pin.
If a door sticks, check the hinges before reaching for a plane, as loose screws let it sag.
If a screw just spins, pack the hole with matchsticks and wood glue, snap them off flush, and drive the screw back in.
Crooked cabinet doors usually have adjustable hinges.
Sealing wet areas.
Look at the sealant where your bath or shower meets the wall.
If it is black with mould, cracked or peeling, water can seep behind it and damage the wall and floor.
Resealing is a satisfying weekend job.
Cut away the old sealant with a sharp blade or a removal tool, clean the joint thoroughly and let it dry completely.
Apply masking tape on either side for a clean edge, then run a steady bead of mould resistant bathroom silicone along the gap.
Smooth it with a wet finger or a shaping tool and peel the tape away straight away.
Let it cure for the time stated on the tube before using the shower.
Good ventilation afterwards keeps the new seal fresh for longer.
The key idea: A small set of quality tools, with safety gear, handles most household jobs.
Part two. Six knots worth knowing.
Most people know one knot and use it for everything.
Sailors, climbers and truckies know better, and a handful of knots will cover almost anything you need.
Terms and the reef knot.
Knot instructions use a small vocabulary.
The working end is the end you move to tie the knot.
The standing part is the rest of the rope, often the part under load.
A bight is a U-shaped fold, and a loop is a bight where the rope crosses itself.
Almost every knot weakens a rope, so climbing or lifting people needs proper training.
The reef knot, or square knot, is right over left, then left over right.
It lies flat, so it suits bandages, slings and parcels.
Get the second step wrong and you have a granny knot, which slips.
To join two ropes under strain, a sheet bend is far more secure, because a reef knot can capsize.
The bowline.
Pronounced ‘boh-lin’, the bowline has been called the king of knots.
It forms a loop at the end of a rope that does not tighten or slide.
That makes it useful for tying a rope around a tree or post, or, in a rescue, a person.
Children learn it with a story: make a small loop, then the rabbit, the working end, comes up out of the hole, around the tree and back down the hole.
After taking a heavy load, a bowline can still be loosened by pushing the collar.
Its weakness is that it can work loose when not under load, so climbers usually prefer a figure-eight loop.
Tying to a post.
The clove hitch is two turns around a pole, the second crossing over the first and tucked under itself.
It is fast to tie and easy to adjust and undo.
It secures boat fenders, starts lashings and ties off tent lines and garden stakes.
It is not set-and-forget: if the post rotates or the load changes direction, it can work loose.
For a long-term tie, add half hitches.
If a rope is already under tension, perhaps from a boat drifting away, use a round turn and two half hitches.
Pass the rope around the object twice, so friction takes most of the load.
Then make a half hitch around the standing part, and repeat it in the same direction.
It is strong, secure and easy to untie after a strain.
Boaties use it for mooring.
Stoppers and tensioners.
A stopper knot keeps a rope from escaping.
An overhand knot works but can jam tight.
The figure-eight is better: make a loop, pass the end around the standing part, then back through the loop.
It is bulkier, so it is less likely to pull through, and easier to untie.
Sailors use it on lines, and it suits drawstrings and clotheslines.
Threaded back along itself, it forms the loop climbers rely on.
The trucker's hitch works like a simple pulley.
Make a fixed loop partway along the rope, pass the working end around an anchor point such as a tie-down hook, then back through the loop.
The mechanical advantage is theoretically about three to one, though friction reduces it.
Pinch it, secure with two half hitches, and recheck the load after a few kilometres.
Practise until hands know.
Reading about knots is a little like reading about swimming.
It only sticks once you have done it many times.
Keep a short length of rope near the couch and tie each knot while watching television until you can do it without looking.
Then practise in awkward conditions: with the rope behind a post, in the dark, or with cold hands.
That is when you will actually need it, while a tarp flaps in a storm or a boat drifts from the jetty.
Start with the bowline, the clove hitch and the round turn with two half hitches.
Those three alone will handle most everyday jobs.
The key idea: Learn the basic rope terms, and remember the reef knot suits bandages and parcels but not joining ropes under load.
Part three. Mending clothes: buttons, seams and holes.
A missing button or a split seam sends a lot of good clothing to landfill.
Ten minutes with a needle and thread can save it.
Make do and mend.
During the Second World War, clothing in Britain was rationed, and in 1943 the government published a booklet called Make Do and Mend.
It taught people to darn socks, patch elbows and make clothes last, as people always had.
Today clothing is cheap and huge amounts end up in landfill, often for faults that take minutes to fix.
Mending is returning to save money, reduce waste and, for many people, to calm the mind.
A useful kit fits in a small tin: hand-sewing needles, thread in black, white, navy, grey and beige, pins, small sharp scissors, safety pins and spare buttons.
A seam ripper makes unpicking easy.
If unsure of a colour, choose slightly darker thread, which shows less.
Thread and buttons.
Cut thread about as long as your arm, as longer lengths tangle.
For jobs that take strain, pull the thread through until the ends meet and knot them, so you sew with a double strand.
Finish with a few small stitches in the same spot to lock it.
To sew on a button, start from the back so the knot is hidden.
Go up through one hole and down the opposite one several times.
Here is the trick most people miss: lay a toothpick or matchstick across the button and sew over it.
Remove it, bring the needle up under the button and wind thread around the stitches.
This forms a shank, so the button sits neatly without puckering.
Seams and hems.
A split seam, perhaps under an arm, is often the quickest fix.
Turn the garment inside out and pin the edges together along the old stitch line.
Start a little before the gap, where the stitching is sound, and sew a backstitch: bring the needle up a short way ahead, then go back down at the end of the previous stitch.
This makes a strong, continuous line.
Carry on past the gap and lock off.
For a dropped hem, fold it back along its crease and pin it.
With a slip stitch, hide the thread inside the fold and pick up just one or two threads of the main fabric each time.
Keep stitches small and not too tight.
Iron-on hemming tape is a quick fix that may not survive many washes.
Darning and visible mending.
Darning is the traditional repair for socks and knitwear.
Stretch the area over something rounded, such as a darning mushroom or a light bulb.
Sew rows of thread across the hole, then weave more threads through them at right angles, creating a small patch of new fabric.
For woven clothes like jeans, a patch on the inside or outside works well.
Many menders now celebrate their repairs rather than hiding them.
Sashiko, a Japanese stitching tradition whose name means roughly ‘little stabs’, uses rows of small running stitches, often white on indigo, to reinforce worn cloth.
Patched and repatched Japanese textiles called boro, once a sign of poverty, are now admired as art.
Zips and knowing limits.
Zips cause a lot of unnecessary clothing deaths.
If a zip sticks, rub a graphite pencil, a bar of soap or a little candle wax along the teeth, then work the slider gently back and forth.
If the teeth keep separating behind the slider, it has often widened with wear.
Squeezing its sides very gently with pliers, a little at a time, can make it grip again.
If a pull tab snaps off, a small key ring or paperclip makes a serviceable replacement.
Some repairs, such as replacing a whole zip in a coat, are fiddly enough that a tailor or alterations shop is worth the money.
Knowing which jobs to do yourself and which to pay for is part of the skill.
The key idea: Mending was once ordinary and is returning, and a small tin of supplies covers most repairs.
Part four. Cleaning smarter: the science of stains.
Hot water can set a bloodstain for good, and vinegar can wreck a marble benchtop.
Learn what is really happening when you clean, and you will clean faster with fewer products.
Why soap works.
Rinse a greasy frying pan under the tap and the water simply beads and runs off, leaving the oil behind.
Oil and water do not mix, which is why plain water is a poor cleaner.
Soaps and detergents solve this with molecules called surfactants.
One end of each is attracted to water, and the other end to oil and grease.
When you scrub, millions of these molecules surround tiny droplets of grease, oily tails pointing in and water-loving heads pointing out.
The grease is wrapped in little parcels that rinse away.
Warm water helps because it softens fats, and scrubbing helps because it breaks grime into smaller pieces for the surfactants to grab.
Order, then disinfect.
Wipe the bench until it gleams, then dust the rangehood and watch crumbs drift onto it.
Professionals avoid this with two rules.
Work top to bottom, so gravity carries dirt onto areas not yet cleaned.
Work dry to wet: dust and vacuum before you mop, because wet cloths turn loose dust into smeared mud.
Spray a product and leave it for a few minutes, since many cleaners need contact time to loosen grime.
Cleaning with detergent and water lifts off dirt, grease and most germs.
Disinfecting uses chemicals to kill the rest, but disinfectants work poorly through grime, so clean first.
Most must stay wet for several minutes, so check the label.
Ordinary cleaning is enough for most of the home.
Save disinfecting for high risk spots, such as benches after raw meat and toilets.
Acids, alkalis, surfaces.
The chalky white crust on a shower screen in a hard water area is mostly alkaline mineral deposit.
A mild acid such as white vinegar or citric acid dissolves it.
Greasy kitchen grime responds better to alkaline products such as bicarbonate of soda or dishwashing detergent.
Knowing this saves you buying a cupboard full of special sprays.
It also protects your surfaces.
Acids etch natural stone such as marble and limestone, leaving dull patches, so use a pH neutral cleaner there.
Mixing vinegar with bicarb, a popular online trick, mostly cancels them out.
The fizz is carbon dioxide, and what remains is largely salty water.
Use each separately, for the job it does best.
Never mix these products.
Some cleaning mistakes leave streaks.
Others put people in hospital.
Bleach, which contains sodium hypochlorite, is the most dangerous product to combine.
Mixed with ammonia, found in some glass and multipurpose cleaners, it releases chloramine gases.
Mixed with acids, including vinegar and some toilet and descaling cleaners, it can release chlorine gas.
Both irritate the eyes and lungs and can cause serious breathing problems.
Even mixing two brands of toilet cleaner can be risky if you do not know what is in them.
The safe habits are simple.
Use one product at a time, rinse between products, keep products in their original labelled bottles, and open a window.
If someone feels unwell after exposure, call the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26.
Know your stain.
Protein stains, such as blood, egg, milk and sweat, need cold water first, because heat cooks the proteins and bonds them to the fibres.
Enzyme pre-treatments then break them down.
Tannin stains, such as tea, coffee, wine and fruit juice, usually respond to prompt rinsing and laundry detergent, though some need an oxygen bleach soak.
Grease needs dishwashing liquid rubbed in before a warm wash.
Dye stains, such as ink, are hardest and may need specialist removers.
On a fresh spill, resist scrubbing, which pushes the stain deeper.
Blot from the outer edge towards the centre.
Test any product on a hidden spot first, and rinse it out afterwards.
Check the stain has gone before using a dryer or iron, as heat can fix a faint stain permanently.
The key idea: Detergent molecules grab grease with one end and water with the other, so grease rinses away.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Which power tool is described as the most useful for a starter kit?
Answer. A cordless drill driver.
Question two. What is the reef knot's main weakness?
Answer. It can capsize if ropes are pulled hard.
Question three. Why is mending making a comeback?
Answer. It saves money, cuts waste and is calming.
Question four. How do detergent molecules remove grease?
Answer. One end holds grease, one holds water.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
